tn_leda.blurb: Leda is a small roadside sandstone crag outside Soddy-Daisy, north of Chattanooga, with a friendly mix of sport lines and traditional routes. The rock is mostly good, and the grades run from the easy 5.6s through the 5.12s, with the bulk of the climbing in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. It works well for newer leaders and for a quick session after work, and a modest trad rack is worth carrying for the crack lines. Some of the easier routes feel stiffer than their numbers suggest, so warm up with a little humility.
tn_leda.parking_note: Use the paved lot at the hairpin bend on Montlake Road, across from Terrace Falls Drive. Space is tight, so carpool when you can. The old roadside pull-offs are not for parking.
tn_leda.approach: A rough cut trail leads up from the lot, passing beneath power lines on the way to the cliff.

tn_lilly_bluff.blurb: Lilly Bluff is a compact sandstone wall in the Obed river gorge, reached by one of the shortest walks in the area. The climbing is mostly bolted sport, with a smaller number of trad lines, and nearly everything sits between 5.10 and 5.12 with a few easier and a couple harder. The wall is shady, which makes it one of the Obed's more popular choices when the weather warms up. Parking is in paved lots on either side of Lilly Bridge, so arrive early on busy weekends.
tn_lilly_bluff.parking_note: Park in one of the two paved lots flanking Lilly Bridge; if they are full, use the Lilly Overlook lots and walk in from there.
tn_lilly_bluff.approach: From the west end of the bridge, a short trail past the trash can follows the cliff line to a tall prominent wall; bear right along the base.

tn_the_camp.blurb: The Camp, also known as the Concentration Camp section, sits in Suck Creek Canyon above the Tennessee River near Chattanooga. The climbing is mainly traditional, with a handful of aid lines, and most routes fall between 5.9 and 5.12 with a few easier ones. Some routes run two pitches, giving the canyon a bit of an adventure feel. The canyon is quieter than the better-known Chattanooga cliffs, but rock quality is variable, so expect the occasional loose or rotten section and test holds before trusting them.

ut_cliffs_of_insanity.blurb: Cliffs of Insanity is a remote wall in the Indian Creek corridor, climbed almost entirely with traditional gear on Wingate sandstone cracks. Most lines fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with very few easy options, which is part of why it sees far fewer people than the roadside walls. Bring a full rack of cams in the hand and finger sizes. Park only on durable surfaces, never on the crusty soil.
ut_cliffs_of_insanity.parking_note: A dirt road runs off opposite the Superbowl campground. A pullout about half a mile in suits a regular car; a high-clearance 4WD can go farther.

ut_green_valley_gap.blurb: Green Valley Gap is a low-elevation sandstone crag on the west side of St. George, popular for short, easy-to-reach sport routes, with some top-rope and trad lines and a few boulder problems. Grades run broadly from 5.7 through 5.12, concentrated in the 5.9 to 5.11 range. Its low position makes it warm, so it suits the cooler seasons better than midsummer. The sandstone is soft and damaged easily when wet, so give it a day or two to dry after rain or snow before pulling on holds.

ut_lower_jungle.blurb: Lower Jungle is a band of broken volcanic cliffs on the Aquarius Plateau at roughly 10,400 feet, among the highest drive-up crags in the country. The routes are mostly long cracks, with a few bolted lines, concentrated between 5.9 and 5.12. Its north-facing position makes it a good afternoon choice once the upper areas have warmed, and fall is the pleasant season. Thunderstorms are common in late summer but often clear by mid-afternoon. Rock quality varies, with loose blocks in places, so check holds and wear a helmet.
ut_lower_jungle.parking_note: A flat rocky pullout on the right side of the forest road, with room for roughly five cars; the road is dirt, and clearance helps.
ut_lower_jungle.approach: A trail climbs a few big steps, crosses a log, then runs north along the cliff base to the routes.

ut_scarface.blurb: Scarface Wall is a well-known Indian Creek crag along the road, climbed entirely with traditional gear on Wingate sandstone cracks. Grades run mostly from 5.10 to 5.12, with the heaviest concentration at 5.11. The wall takes its name from its most famous line, a clean finger-to-hand crack. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons in the Creek, since most walls there bake in summer. Park only on hard ground, never on the crusty soil, and carry out all waste because toilets are scarce.
